strengths: The core idea of using continuation log-probability (MCLP) from a pretrained LALM as a proxy for stylistic consistency is simple, interpretable, and practically useful, addressing a genuine bottleneck (lack of objective style metrics and dense rewards) in expressive TTS.

The hybrid reward design (MCLP + CER with a gating mechanism) is well-motivated, and the reward-hacking ablations (Table 3) are convincing: style-only optimization produces gibberish with high MCLP, content-only optimization regresses style — this directly validates the necessity of the composite reward.
The human–metric consistency analysis (Figure 5) provides evidence that MCLP correlates with human judgments of style consistency, with win rate rising above 0.8 for large ΔMCLP.

A substantial new RP-TTS dataset (~311k scenes, ~1,435 hours, multi-turn, scene/character annotations) with a documented curation pipeline, dataset statistics, and a video-level train/test split to prevent leakage; construction prompts are provided in the appendix.
Ablations of SFT vs. RL stages clarify the contribution of each component, and the paper is generally clearly organized with a worked example (Figure 2) and formalized problem statement.
weaknesses: Circularity between metric and reward: the proposed model is directly optimized to maximize MCLP, so its MCLP superiority in Table 2 is partly by construction. While the MOS result mitigates this, the entanglement of the 'MCLP is a good metric' claim and the 'MCLP is a good reward' claim is never fully disentangled.

MCLP as a metric is not validated against confounds. Since z_eval and z_gt share identical transcripts, MCLP may partially capture acoustic/tokenizer artifacts, timbre, or channel characteristics rather than style per se. There is no controlled experiment (e.g., fixed style with different speakers, or fixed speaker with different styles) demonstrating that MCLP isolates style rather than speaker identity or audio quality.
The paper claims MCLP is superior to emotion-classification rewards, but this competing reward is never implemented or compared empirically — only motivated argumentatively in Section 2.3.

The subjective evaluation is small: 31 samples, 30 valid responses, one gold-standard filter. The headline claim that MOS 3.646 'approaches ground truth naturalness' (4.411) rests on a limited sample; no standard correlation coefficient (e.g., Spearman) is reported for Figure 5, only binned win rates with wide confidence intervals.

Baseline fairness concerns: all baselines (including closed-source GPT-Audio) are resynthesized through the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer with ground-truth audio prompts, which may disadvantage them; the very low GPT-Audio MOS (1.75) suggests possible artifacts of this procedure rather than genuine model quality.

The information-theoretic justification (Eq. 2–3) is heuristic: the KL direction, the 'strong density estimator' assumption, and the claim that MI variation is dominated by style are asserted rather than tested; the analysis does not predict any falsifiable behavior that is subsequently verified.

Generalization is narrow: all results use a single backbone (Step-Audio-2-mini) on Mandarin data; no evidence that MCLP works as a reward with other LALMs or languages. The RL data filtering uses an 'internal style classification model' that is neither described nor released, hurting reproducibility.

Dataset annotations are produced by DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-VL without any reported quality assessment (e.g., human verification of scene/character description accuracy), and the dataset is only 'will be open source' with no code or metric release confirmed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: objective evaluation and reward design for stylistic consistency in multi-turn Role-Play TTS, a task existing emotion-classifier-based RL rewards handle poorly.

The proposed MCLP metric is simple, computable, and the information-theoretic motivation (likelihood of ground-truth continuation as a proxy for stylistic mutual information) is a plausible and interpretable framing.

The gated hybrid reward (MCLP + CER) is well motivated, and the reward-hacking ablations (style-only optimization producing 'expressive gibberish' with CER > 50%; content-only optimization regressing style below the SFT baseline) are informative and honestly reported.

The constructed RP-TTS dataset (311k scenes, ~1,435 hours, multi-turn with scene and character annotations, video-level train/test split) is a substantial resource, and the data curation pipeline and prompts are documented in the appendix.
Human-metric consistency analysis (win-rate vs. ΔMCLP bins with 95% CIs) shows a clear monotonic trend, providing some empirical support for the metric's alignment with human judgment.
weaknesses: Validity of MCLP as a *style* metric is not convincingly established. Because the transcript is held fixed, higher likelihood of ground-truth tokens conditioned on the evaluation audio may be dominated by speaker/timbre similarity and acoustic quality rather than stylistic attributes like prosody or emotion. No control experiment (e.g., same-speaker/different-style vs. different-speaker/same-style) isolates style from timbre, and MCLP itself is computed on non-resynthesized audio, unlike the MOS evaluation where this confound was addressed. This is the paper's central claim and it remains under-supported.

The information-theoretic justification is heuristic. The claim that minimizing conditional entropy is 'asymptotically equivalent' to maximizing expected log-likelihood, the loose KL divergence assumptions, and the assertion that MI variation is 'dominated by style' are asserted rather than demonstrated, and the derivation does not account for the shared content conditioning.

The reward model and the policy share the same backbone (Step-Audio-2-mini-Base), creating an entanglement between the metric and the optimized system: RL could exploit density-estimation quirks of the same model family, and the general applicability of MCLP to other LALMs is untested.

The human study is very small: 31 samples and 30 valid annotator responses. The correlation analysis is built entirely on pairwise comparisons within this tiny set, with no comparison against alternative reference metrics (e.g., emotion classifiers, speaker-similarity, other likelihood variants), so the claimed superiority of MCLP as a metric is not demonstrated relative to baselines.
MCLP requires ground-truth reference audio, so it is not a reference-free metric; its usefulness as a general evaluation tool outside settings where GT audio exists is unclear and not discussed.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: GPT-Audio's CER of 44.7% in the cold-start setting is suspiciously poor, ASR-based CER is computed with the authors' own fine-tuned ASR model, and all baselines are evaluated without equivalent fine-tuning on the RP-TTS task, so gains may partly reflect in-domain adaptation rather than the proposed method.
The claim that the proposed system 'approaches the naturalness of the ground truth' is overstated: MOS 3.646 vs. 4.411 for ground truth is a large gap.

Data ethics treatment is thin: the dataset is derived from copyrighted YouTube drama content (audio, video frames, and subtitles) with only automated (Qwen-VL/DeepSeek) annotation and no reported human verification of annotation quality; the impact statement is boilerplate and does not address IP or consent issues.

Reproducibility gaps: the internal style classifier used for RL data filtering is not described or released, hyperparameter sensitivity (C, λ, τ) is unexplored, and the dataset is only 'promised' open source. No statistical significance is reported for objective metrics.

strengths: The core idea of MCLP—using a pretrained LALM's continuation likelihood of ground-truth tokens as a style-consistency signal—is simple, interpretable, and well-motivated; the paper clearly articulates why emotion-classification rewards are insufficient for RP-TTS.
The information-theoretic framing (Eq. 2–3), while heuristic, gives a principled rationale for why MCLP should proxy stylistic mutual information when transcripts are held constant.

The paper honestly addresses reward hacking and includes a valuable ablation (Table 3) showing style-only optimization collapses intelligibility (CER > 59%) while content-only optimization regresses style below the SFT baseline—this is convincing evidence that the gated hybrid reward is necessary.

The human–metric consistency analysis (Figure 5) is a sensible validation design: binning pairwise ΔMCLP and showing win rate rises from ~0.5 to >0.8 for ΔMCLP > 0.1 directly tests the central claim that MCLP tracks human judgment.

The dataset construction pipeline (Figure 3, Appendix A) is described in actionable detail (prompts included), with a video-level train/test split to prevent leakage, and the paper commits to open-sourcing the data.

Results are strong across both content and style metrics, including a cold-start (no audio history) setting where baselines degrade badly; the claimed use of acoustic history is supported by the +0.051 MCLP gain in the history setting.
weaknesses: The subjective evaluation is very small: only 31 curated samples (30 valid responses) underpin the MOS results, yet the abstract claims the method 'significantly outperforms strong LALM baselines' on subjective metrics. MOS with 95% CIs on 30 responses from 32 annotators is thin evidence for a headline claim; more samples and statistical tests (e.g., paired tests against baselines) are needed.

There is a circularity risk in the evaluation: MCLP is computed with Step-Audio-2-mini-Base, the same model family that is both the generator backbone and the RL reward source. Optimizing against a scorer and then reporting that scorer as an objective metric invites self-preference bias. The human-MOS correlation partially mitigates this, but the correlation analysis is itself based on small samples, and the paper does not test MCLP with an independent scorer LALM or report sensitivity of results to the choice of scoring model.

The information-theoretic justification (Eq. 3) relies on the assumption that the pretrained LALM is a strong density estimator (small KL term) and that MI variation is 'dominated by style attributes' given identical transcripts. The latter is asserted, not shown—likelihood could also be influenced by speaking rate/duration alignment with the reference, tokenization artifacts, or acoustic channel effects, none of which are isolated experimentally (e.g., MCLP of the GT against itself, or of re-synthesized GT with mismatched style, is not reported).

Dataset annotation quality is unverified: scene descriptions come from Qwen-VL and character profiles from DeepSeek-R1 with no reported human validation of annotation accuracy or noise rates, even though these annotations define the very task (style alignment with S and P).

Reproducibility gaps: the 'internal style classification model' used to filter the RL subset is not described or released; the RL filtering (Not-Neutral only) could confound comparisons since training data distribution differs across stages; only a promise that the dataset 'will be open source'.

Some experimental details raise fairness questions: baseline samples are resynthesized via the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer (⋄) for subjective evaluation; the procedure and its effect on baseline audio quality are not analyzed, and MOS gaps vs. baselines (e.g., 3.646 vs. 2.471) are large enough that tokenizer artifacts could contribute.

The paper lacks discussion of limitations (no limitations section), including the metric's dependence on the scoring LALM, its language coverage (Chinese-only evaluation), and the risk that RL overfits to the scorer's stylistic distribution rather than genuinely improving role-play expressiveness.

strengths: MCLP is a simple, well-motivated, and interpretable metric that repurposes the ICL capability of pretrained LALMs to quantify stylistic consistency, and it is convincingly dual-purposed as both an evaluation metric and a dense RL reward signal.

The paper directly anticipates and empirically demonstrates reward hacking: the 'w/o CER Reward' ablation shows catastrophic intelligibility breakdown (CER > 50%) with the highest MCLP, and the gated hybrid reward resolves this trade-off — a well-designed and honest set of ablations (Table 3).

Large-scale dataset construction (1,435 hours, 311k scenes) from real drama videos with a careful video-level test split to prevent leakage, stratified sampling, and a documented annotation pipeline (prompts in Appendix A).

Human validation of the metric is thoughtful: the win-rate-vs-ΔMCLP analysis (Figure 5) shows a monotone trend exceeding 0.8 win rate for ΔMCLP > 0.1, with QC via gold-standard insertions and filtering of inconsistent annotators.

Comprehensive baseline coverage spanning closed-source (GPT-Audio), open multi-turn LALMs (MiMo-Audio, Step-Audio-2-mini), and Instruct-TTS systems, evaluated under both w/ and w/o audio-history settings, plus fine-grained analyses by scene category, dialogue length, and speaker count (Appendix C) and a cross-lingual sanity check (Appendix B).
Honest limitations section covering Mandarin-only scope, domain coverage, and LLM-generated annotation noise, and an impact statement addressing misuse risks.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/bias in MCLP as an evaluation metric: the MCLP scorer is a continuation model built on Step-Audio-2 with its TA4 tokenizer, and the proposed system is itself a Step-Audio-2-family model trained (SFT + RL) to optimize MCLP. Baselines from other model families are scored through a scorer that shares the authors' tokenizer and distributional priors, raising the concern that MCLP systematically favors the authors' model family. The 'Resys' row in Appendix B (tokenizer-reconstructed GT scoring far below raw GT) suggests non-trivial tokenizer sensitivity, which is not analyzed in depth.

The human correlation study (32 listeners) is described only at a high level: it is unclear which systems' outputs were used to form pairs, how many pairs fall in each ΔMCLP bin, and no standard correlation statistics (Spearman/Kendall) are reported; the headline 'aligned with human judgments' claim rests on a relatively small and partially unspecified study.
The subjective MOS evaluation is small (30 test cases, 48 valid annotators), and the protocol's new 'stylistic consistency MOS' is not externally validated or released in enough detail to reproduce.

Reproducibility gaps: the internal 'style classification model' used to filter the RL dataset is not described; the code URL in the abstract is blank; hyperparameters C, λ, τ are given without sensitivity analysis; and legality/licensing of redistributing 1,435 hours of YouTube drama content derived from WenetSpeech is not addressed.

The MOS gain from MCLP-based RL over SFT alone (+0.398) is meaningful but modest relative to the large SFT gain (+1.32), and since the SFT stage already uses in-domain data absent from all baselines, the relative contribution of the MCLP reward versus in-domain fine-tuning could be more sharply isolated.

Some baseline results invite scrutiny (e.g., GPT-Audio's 44.7% CER in the w/o-history setting), and the paper does not detail prompt-construction for closed-source baselines, leaving open the possibility of under-tuned comparisons.

strengths: The core idea — using the continuation log-probability of a pretrained LALM as an objective stylistic-consistency metric and RL reward — is a sensible and interpretable alternative to discrete emotion-classification rewards, and the paper is one of the first to target stylistic consistency in multi-turn Role-Play TTS specifically.
The correlation analysis in Figure 5 (win rate vs. ΔMCLP binned over pairs) is a reasonable attempt to validate the metric against human judgments, showing win rates above 0.8 for ΔMCLP > 0.1.

The ablation study (Table 3) is informative and honest: it demonstrates reward hacking when optimizing MCLP alone (CER > 50%) and stylistic collapse when optimizing CER alone, motivating the gated hybrid reward.

The paper constructs a large annotated RP-TTS dataset (1,435 hours, ~311k scenes) with a documented multi-stage pipeline, video-level train/test split to avoid leakage, and detailed prompts in the appendix; limitations (Mandarin-only, LLM annotation noise, domain coverage) are explicitly discussed, and an impact statement is provided.
Human evaluation uses 50 trained annotators with a gold-standard quality-control case and reports 95% confidence intervals on MOS.
weaknesses: Circularity / self-evaluation bias: the MCLP metric is computed by a continuation model trained by the authors on 3M hours, and then the proposed model is trained (via GRPO) to maximize MCLP and is evaluated using MCLP. Gains on MCLP (-4.753 → -4.636) are therefore partly an artifact of optimizing the evaluation metric itself. The human-MOS validation (Fig. 5) is conducted on the same domain and pipelines, so it does not fully de-bias the headline metric results.

The claim that the metric is 'conceptually symmetric' is asserted rather than demonstrated; predicting GT tokens from a candidate context is inherently asymmetric (e.g., candidate length/content differences can affect continuation likelihood in ways not tied to style), and no analysis quantifies this confound.

Subjective evaluation is thin relative to the central claim: only 30 test cases (with Instruct-TTS baselines evaluated on fewer), and annotators are instructed to disregard timbre and audio quality. The '⋄' resynthesis of baseline outputs through the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer raises fairness concerns — this procedure could degrade baseline audio/style and does not clearly disentangle style from quality as claimed. No naturalness MOS is reported at all.

Several quantitative claims are weakly supported: MCLP differences between systems are small (e.g., -4.636 vs. -4.637 in Table 3) with no significance testing; fine-grained analyses in Appendix C use very small subsets (e.g., 4 scenes with 5 speakers, 8 animation scenes), yet 'best in all categories' conclusions are drawn.

Baseline results appear suspicious in places (GPT-Audio CER of 44.7% in the w/o-history setting), suggesting possible prompt-format mismatch rather than genuine capability differences; no effort is made to verify or tune baselines to the task.

Novelty is moderate: likelihood-based continuation scores have known precedents in speech and language evaluation, and the RL recipe (GRPO + hybrid reward with ASR gating) is standard; the main novelty is the domain-specific application and dataset.

Reproducibility and ethics concerns: the dataset is built from copyrighted Chinese drama videos scraped from YouTube with LLM-generated scene/character annotations, and the paper does not discuss licensing/redistribution rights for releasing this data; annotation noise is acknowledged but not quantified. The code release URL is a placeholder in the submission.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: using the continuation log-probability of a pretrained LALM (MCLP) as a reference-based proxy for stylistic consistency, which addresses a genuine gap since existing RL for TTS relies on coarse emotion-classifier rewards.

The metric is validated against human judgments with a careful win-rate analysis (Figure 5) across ∆MCLP bins with 95% CIs, showing a clean monotone trend (win rate > 0.8 for ∆MCLP > 0.1), which supports the central claim that MCLP tracks human perception of stylistic consistency.

The composite reward design (MCLP + CER with gated aggregation) is sensible, and the ablations in Table 3 are convincing: optimizing MCLP alone produces severe reward hacking (CER > 50% with the highest MCLP score), while CER alone yields flat speech (MOS 2.331 vs. 3.576). This directly demonstrates why the hybrid reward is needed.

Substantial experimental effort: comparisons against strong multi-turn LALMs (GPT-Audio, MiMo-Audio-7B) and Instruct-TTS systems, a dedicated subjective protocol with 50 trained annotators, gold-standard quality control, and fine-grained analyses across scene categories, dialogue lengths, and speaker counts (Appendix C).
The paper is transparent about limitations (Mandarin-only main evaluation, LLM-generated annotation noise) and includes an impact statement addressing misuse risks of expressive speech generation.

A cross-lingual sanity check (Appendix B, Table 4) shows MCLP consistently prefers self-prompted over prev-prompted synthesis in both English and Mandarin, providing some evidence the metric generalizes beyond the training domain.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the metric: MCLP is computed by a Step-Audio-2-based continuation model, ground-truth samples in the subjective evaluation are resynthesized through the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer (the '⋄' protocol), and the proposed model is fine-tuned on data drawn from the same distribution. MCLP scores may partially reflect token-distribution familiarity with the authors' own pipeline rather than purely style consistency; a metric computed by a differently tokenized LALM would strengthen the claims.

MCLP is inherently reference-based: it measures continuation likelihood of ground-truth audio given candidate audio for the same transcript. As an evaluation metric for 'instruction following' of scene/character descriptions this is only meaningful when a matching GT reference exists, which limits applicability to open-ended role-play settings where no GT audio is available. The paper does not discuss this limitation explicitly.

The continuation model is trained on 3 million hours of speech, and the RL data filtering uses an 'internal style classification model.' These choices make both the metric and the data pipeline difficult to reproduce exactly; the code-release URL appears incomplete and dataset release terms (WenetSpeech-derived YouTube videos) are not discussed.

The proposed model is trained (SFT + RL) on in-domain Chinese drama data while baselines are general-purpose models, so part of the large MOS/MCLP gap over baselines reflects domain-specific fine-tuning rather than the MCLP reward alone; a fairer control (e.g., SFT/RL on the same data with an alternative style reward such as emotion-classifier rewards mentioned in Section 2.3) is missing.

The subjective correlation study is modest in scale (32 listeners for the MCLP correlation, 30 test cases for MOS, 48 valid responses), and only win-rate analysis is reported — standard rank correlations (Spearman/Kendall) between MCLP and MOS would make the alignment claim easier to compare with prior metric-validation work.
The English/Mandarin generalization test uses a proxy task (self- vs. prev-prompted TTS) rather than human validation, so cross-lingual claims remain preliminary, as the authors acknowledge.
